extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, writers, and educated readers interested in aesthetics and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for writing and evaluating literary criticism and for understanding the critic's creative role; discusses how critics should treat works of art and how literature differs from other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism_as_a_creative_art
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism is itself an art: creative, independent, and capable of producing work as flawless and beautiful as poetry or painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic works with materials and puts them into a new form; he does not need fine materials (anything will serve). Examples: from the trivial (Royal Academy pictures, mediocre novels or plays) a true critic can produce work 'flawless in beauty and instinct with intellectual subtlety.' Criticism is a 'creation within a creation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence_over_imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should not be judged by standards of imitation or resemblance; criticism need not reproduce or echo the original work’s form or intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism is not to be measured by how closely it mirrors the artist's work; like the artist to the visible world, the critic occupies a distinct relation to the work. The critic can create from 'sordid and sentimental' subjects as artists do; 'treatment is the test.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment_is_the_test
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter matters less than treatment: anything can be transformed into fine criticism by the critic’s handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gustave Flaubert turning trivial provincial life into classic style; the critic can make masterpieces from insignificant subjects. The critic's pleasure and faculty of contemplation determine the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest_criticism_as_personal_impression
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest criticism is the purest form of personal impression — a record of the critic’s own soul — and is thus more creative in that it has least reference to external standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of criticism is 'in itself, and to itself, an end.' It is not trammelled by verisimilitude or probability and may appeal from fiction unto fact but not from the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism_impressive_not_expressive
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should treat works of art as starting points for new impressions rather than attempting to recover the artist's original expressive intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The highest criticism 'deals with art not as expressive but as impressive purely.' The critic may attribute meanings and associations to a work that the artist never intended (e.g., the critic’s interpretation of the Mona Lisa), and this is a legitimate and high form of criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity_of_meaning_and_suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Valued art and criticism produce suggestion and allow many interpretations; works that are too explicit or merely illustrative are less interesting to the critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictures that are intelligible illustrations 'rank with illustrations' and 'do not stir the imagination.' The critic prefers works that 'possess the subtle quality of suggestion' and 'seem to tell one that even from them there is an escape into a wider world.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Value_of_limitations_and_incompleteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Renunciation or limitation (of colour, dimension, literal realism) is valuable: by being incomplete, art achieves a richer unity and addresses the aesthetic sense rather than reason alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sculptor surrenders imitative colour, painter surrenders actual dimensions; through incompleteness art avoids mere imitation or pure intellectualism and produces 'a pure synthetic impression.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic_as_interpreter_requires_scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: When acting as an interpreter, the critic must ground interpretations in broad scholarship: historical context, language, genre history, and the conditions that shaped the original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand Shakespeare truly one must know Renaissance and Reformation relations, Elizabethan theatre conditions, the history of verse forms, Greek drama, and more — binding Elizabethan London to Athens to find Shakespeare’s true position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality_is_essential_for_interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic’s strong and individual personality is not a disturbance but a revelation; the more the critic’s personality enters the interpretation, the more real and convincing it becomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: musicians and actors give us their own reading of Beethoven or Hamlet; Rubinstein gives 'Beethoven and also himself.' The critic must 'intensify [his] own individualism' to interpret others effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical_reproduction_should_be_transformative_not_imitative
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic reproduces the work he criticises in a new, non-imitative mode that transforms the original into literature (or into the critic’s medium), thereby revealing meaning and mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons: etcher as critic of painting, actor as critic of drama; the critic’s reproduction may reject resemblance and gain charm through that rejection, 'transforming each art into literature' to achieve unity among the arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature_can_realize_movement_and_time
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature uniquely realizes movement, the sequence of time, growth, and change — things static arts (statue, painting) cannot truly show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: painting is concentrated to a moment; literature shows seasons, youth, manhood, aging, and the passage of time; therefore movement, 'that problem of the visible arts,' can be truly realised by literature alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art_should_preserve_mystery_over_absolute_realisation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an artist realises an ideal too absolutely, the work loses wonder and mystery; preserving incompleteness or suggestion retains value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'true tragedy' is artists who 'realise their ideal too absolutely,' robbing it of wonder; music is perfect because it 'can never reveal its ultimate secret.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty_as_symbol_and_open-endedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty has many meanings and serves as 'the symbol of symbols': because it 'expresses nothing' it can reveal everything, allowing diverse moods to be projected onto it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty's open-endedness lets each beholder lend meanings; examples include how music or the Mona Lisa can suggest widely different emotions or narratives to different viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's_primary_aim_to_deepen_wonder_not_simplify
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic’s aim is often to deepen the mystery and intensify the majesty of the work rather than to reduce it to a single explanation or the artist’s supposed intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic may 'seek rather to deepen its mystery' and make the work 'more marvellous in the eyes of men.' Ordinary attempts to 'see the object as in itself it really is' miss the critic’s higher province.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism_may_employ_any_materials
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic need not require the best or appropriate materials to produce great work; the critic's art lies in treatment, not in the intrinsic worth of his subject or materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilde argues that even 'sordid and sentimental amours' or trivial gallery pictures may be turned into masterpieces by a creative critic; 'anything will serve his purpose.'
